reason: 'Forced it to endurance' inverts the natural verb construction (forced X to endure); it reads as stilted on a first hearing even though the meaning is recoverable.

old: Anyone else would trust a weaker ally than me, even if that ally were only mortal and less wise than I am.
new: Someone else would trust an ally weaker than me, even an ordinary mortal who was less wise than I am.
reason: Two stacked comparatives ('weaker ally than me' and 'less wise than I am') in one sentence, plus the conditional 'even if that ally were only mortal,' are hard to parse in a single pass aloud. The reworded version keeps the same a-fortiori argument with a slightly flatter parse.

old: Just so, I wish the heavenly gods would hide me from mortal sight, or that Artemis would strike me down.
new: In the same way, I wish the heavenly gods would hide me from mortal sight, or that Artemis would strike me down.
reason: 'Just so' as a stand-alone connector meaning 'in the same way [as those daughters]' is an archaic transitional usage; a contemporary reader is more likely to read it as 'exactly' or miss the callback to the Pandareus story entirely.

old: it puzzled him—it seemed as if she already knew him and was beside him.
new: it puzzled him—it seemed as though she already recognized him and was standing right beside him.
reason: 'Knew him and was beside him' is ambiguous on first read: it could mean she recognized him as her husband, or simply that she was physically near him (which she already was, sleeping in the house). The clarified verb ('recognized') removes the double reading without adding any fact not already implied.
